claim: Intrinsic confidence measures from generative code-LLMs are poorly aligned with actual code correctness out of the box, with Expected Calibration Error (ECE) ranging from 0.09 to 0.73 across tasks, datasets, and models.
stance_target: Code-LLM confidence is not inherently well-calibrated, motivating post-hoc calibration/uncertainty research
scope_conditions: Three tasks (line-level code completion, function synthesis, program repair), five datasets (SStubs, DyPyBench, Defects4J, HumanEval, MBPP), three models (GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct, OpenAI Codex, CodeGen2-16B), temperature 0 sampling
quoted_support: We observe generally high ECE (Expected Calibration Error...) across all settings, ranging from 0.09 to 0.73, suggesting intrinsic LLM confidences are poor predictors of code correctness.

claim: GPT-3.5 line completions with average per-token confidence above 90% pass all test cases only 52% of the time, illustrating severe overconfidence.
stance_target: Code-LLM confidence scores are unreliable proxies for correctness
scope_conditions: GPT-3.5, line-level code completion task, thousands of completions tested
quoted_support: when we test thousands of line completions, in cases where the average probability was greater than 90%, only 52% actually passed test cases.

claim: Platt scaling (logistic-regression rescaling) generally improves measured calibration of code-LLM confidence but can produce a 'bucket collapse' artifact where a poorly-aligned confidence measure gets rescaled to the baseline correctness rate for all samples, yielding a deceptively low ECE near 0 that does not reflect real predictive utility.
stance_target: ECE alone is a sufficient metric for evaluating post-hoc calibration methods
scope_conditions: Post-hoc Platt scaling applied to intrinsic and reflective confidence measures across code generation tasks
quoted_support: If a confidence measure is poorly aligned with correctness, Platt-scaling can rescale (squash) all the confidence values to the baseline rate; this places all samples in a single confidence value bucket where probability exactly matches the baseline rate of correctness, resulting in an ECE near 0.

claim: Rescaling parameters fit via Platt scaling do not generalize well across tasks of different domains: fitting on DyPyBench (program repair) and applying to function synthesis tasks degrades Skill Score from 0.12 to -1.28 and worsens ECE from 0.08 to 0.54, whereas cross-task transfer within the same domain (function synthesis to function synthesis) only mildly degrades performance (SS 0.14->0.12, ECE 0.07->0.05).
stance_target: Calibration methods for code-LLMs must be domain/task-specific and do not transfer robustly across task types
scope_conditions: GPT-3.5, p_NB and p_total confidence measures, function synthesis and program repair tasks
quoted_support: applying the p_total rescaling fit on DyPyBench to the function synthesis tasks, results in an average SS change of 0.12 to -1.28 and ECE change of 0.08 to 0.54, indicating a lack of robustness.

claim: Retrieval-augmented few-shotting substantially improves calibration of GPT-3.5's confidence on code completion, reaching a Skill Score of 0.15, the best result reported in the paper.
stance_target: Reflective/in-context-learning approaches can meaningfully improve code-LLM calibration
scope_conditions: GPT-3.5, code completion task, retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting
quoted_support: calibration improves substantially, reaching a skill score of 0.15, particularly with retrieval augmented few-shotting.

claim: The paper explicitly leaves open whether its findings generalize to models with substantially different architectures or training/fine-tuning regimes beyond the three tested models (GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct, Codex, CodeGen2-16B).
stance_target: Generalizability of code-LLM miscalibration findings across model families
quoted_support: Results might not generalize to all models, especially those with greatly differing training/finetuning or different architectures.

claim: This paper is, to the authors' knowledge, the first to study calibration in a real-world generative code-generation setting, distinguishing it from prior calibration work that focused on non-generative classification settings or natural-language tasks using older-generation models (BERT, RoBERTa, T5).
stance_target: Novelty positioning of code-LLM calibration research prior to 2024
scope_conditions: Related work comparison as of ICSE 2025 submission
quoted_support: To our knowledge, our paper is the first to consider the problem of calibration in a real-world code generation setting.

claim: HumanEval (164 samples) and Defects4J (120 samples) are explicitly flagged by the authors as too small for results on those datasets to reliably generalize, while DyPyBench, SStubs, and MBPP each exceed 800 samples.
stance_target: Dataset scale limitations in code-LLM calibration evaluation
scope_conditions: Sample sizes as used in the ICSE 2025 study
quoted_support: While three of our datasets contain more than 800+ samples each, HumanEval and Defects4J datasets consist of only 164 and 120 samples, respectively. Results on these datasets may not generalize.

claim: Reflective verbalized self-ask confidence (p_v) is generally uncorrelated with logit-based reflective confidence measures (p_B, p_NB), which themselves are strongly positively correlated with each other since derived from similar computations.
stance_target: Relationship between verbalized and logit-based confidence elicitation methods
scope_conditions: RQ3 analysis across function synthesis and program repair tasks
quoted_support: The reflective verbalized self-ask confidence measure p_v, and the two logit-based reflective confidence measures have no consistent relationships.
